title: Fix the 'command not found' error in the terminal
summary: The terminal says 'command not found' when it cannot find a program with the name you typed. The usual causes are a typo, a program that is not installed, or a folder that is missing from the search path. These steps check each cause and show how to find the package that provides the program.

prerequisites: You have the exact message, for example: bash: nosuchtool: command not found
For the package search step: apt-file on Debian, Ubuntu and Mint, or pkgfile on Arch, is installed and its database is updated (see the linked cards)

steps.explain: Read the program name in the message. In 'bash: nosuchtool: command not found' the name is nosuchtool; zsh, the default shell on macOS, says 'zsh: command not found: nosuchtool'. Look for a typo such as gti instead of git and retype the command.
Ask the shell where it finds a program with that name. A path such as /usr/bin/git means the program is installed. No output means the shell cannot find it.

placeholders.name: COMMAND
placeholders.description: The program name from the error message

steps.expect: A path such as /usr/bin/git, or no output at all when the program is not installed.

alternatives.explain: The same check, but it also tells you whether the name is an alias, a shell function or a built-in command.

placeholders.name: COMMAND
placeholders.description: The program name from the error message

alternatives.expect: 'git is /usr/bin/git' when the program is installed, or a 'not found' message when it is not.

steps.explain: Show the folders the shell searches for programs, separated by colons. A program installed in a folder that is not in this list cannot be started by its name. Usual folders are /usr/bin and /bin.

Find the package that contains the program. On Linux, the search tool for your system looks up the file name; on macOS, brew search looks up Homebrew package names. Install the package you find with your package manager; if the search tool itself is missing, install it first (see the linked cards).

placeholders.name: COMMAND
placeholders.description: The program name from the error message

steps.expect: A line that names a package next to the file path, for example tree: /usr/bin/tree on Ubuntu. Nothing printed means no package provides that name.
